The same physical switch carries three separate logical broadcast domains.
A VLAN forms a logical Layer-2 group. Devices in the same VLAN share a broadcast domain even when the grouping does not follow physical location.
Possible limitations without VLANs
A broadcast may reach
every connected section
User groups are not
logically separated
Organisation depends on
physical connections
Unrelated traffic shares
one broadcast domain
Moving a device may
need physical changes
Note: a VLAN supports traffic segmentation, but it is not a complete cybersecurity solution by itself.
VLANs divide one physical switching infrastructure into multiple logical Layer-2 networks.

IEEE 802.1Q VLAN Tag
Untagged frame
Dest Source EtherType Payload FCS
Max untagged frame = 1518 bytes
VLAN-tagged frame
Dest Source 802.1Q Tag EtherType Payload FCS
Max single-tagged frame = 1522 bytes (IEEE 802.1Q tag = 4 bytes)
Information inside the tag
16 bits
TPID
Marks an 802.1Q tag. TPID = 0x8100,
itself an EtherType value.
3 bits
PCP
Priority marking 0–7. Queue mapping
and scheduling policy determine
service order.
1 bit
DEI
Drop eligibility.
12 bits
VLAN ID
Identifies the VLAN. 0 = priority-
tagged, 4095 reserved; usable 1-
4094.
IEEE 802.1Q adds VLAN identity and priority marking. PCP alone does not guarantee latency or transmission order.
VLAN-Tagged Frame Example
Received frame information
Destination MAC = 00:10:20:30:40:50
Source MAC = 00:AA:BB:CC:DD:EE
TPID = 0x8100
VLAN ID = 30
EtherType = 0x0800
Payload = IPv4 packet
Interpretation
1The frame carries an IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tag
2The frame belongs to VLAN 30
3The payload after the tag is an IPv4 packet
4A VLAN-aware switch uses the VLAN ID with its forwarding
information
5The frame is processed within the VLAN 30 broadcast domain

Knowledge Check 5
Question 1
What is the main purpose of a VLAN?
•A. Increase the bits in a MAC address
•B. Create logical Layer-2 networks
•C. Replace the Ethernet PHY
•D. Remove all Ethernet broadcasts
Question 2
Which link commonly carries frames of multiple VLANs?
•A. Simplex link
•B. Access link
•C. Trunk link
•D. Analogue link
Question 3
How many bytes are added by a single IEEE 802.1Q tag?
•A. 2 bytes
•B. 4 bytes
•C. 6 bytes
•D. 12 bytes
Question 4
Can two devices in different VLANs communicate directly at Layer 2?
•A. Yes, always
•B. No, it requires a Layer-3 function
•C. Yes, with the same MAC address
•D. Yes, if they use different switches
Answers
1. B 2. C 3. B 4. B
Why these answers
A VLAN creates a logical Layer-2 network on shared switching hardware. A trunk
link carries several VLANs using tagged frames. The IEEE 802.1Q tag adds 4
bytes. Traffic between VLANs needs a Layer-3 routing function.
Complete Ethernet Communication Flow
End-to-End process
Application creates data
TCP or UDP adds transport info
IP adds logical addresses
Ethernet adds MAC addresses
Ethernet adds EtherType and FCS
PHY converts frame to signals
Switch receives the frame
Switch learns the source MAC
Switch examines destination MAC
Switch forwards, floods or filters
Receiving PHY recovers the bits
Receiving MAC checks the frame
EtherType identifies the protocol
Payload moves up the stack
Destination application receives data
Ethernet combines physical transmission, framing, addressing, switching and error detection to move higher-layer data across a local network.
Common Misconceptions
1. Ethernet and the Internet are the same
Ethernet provides local physical and data-link communication. The
Internet depends on IP communication across interconnected
networks.
2. A switch forwards using IP addresses
A Layer-2 switch forwards frames using destination MAC addresses.
3. The Ethernet frame is inside the IP packet
The IP packet is carried inside the Ethernet frame payload.
4. CSMA/CD is used on every link
CSMA/CD belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not normal full-
duplex switched links.
5. FCS corrects a corrupted frame
FCS supports error detection only. It does not correct corrupted data.
6. A VLAN is a separate physical switch
A VLAN is a logical Layer-2 network that may exist within shared
switching infrastructure.
7. A VLAN alone provides security
VLANs support segmentation, but additional network and
cybersecurity controls are required.

Summary
Ethernet fundamentals established
•Ethernet operates primarily at OSI Layers 1 and 2
•The PHY transmits and receives physical signals
•The MAC creates and processes frames
•MAC addresses support local Layer-2 delivery
•Modern Ethernet uses switched full-duplex links
•Switches learn source MAC addresses
•Switches forward using destination MAC addresses
•Unicast, multicast and broadcast are delivery types
•Frames carry addressing, payload type, data and FCS
•Padding supports the minimum frame size
•FCS supports error detection
•VLANs create separate logical broadcast domains
•IEEE 802.1Q adds VLAN identity and priority
